Global Warming and Climate Change

The summer of 2024 was the hottest ever recorded on Earth, and it was the first calendar year in which the global average temperature was more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. In India, temperatures crossed 50 °C in parts of Rajasthan and Delhi, and heat waves killed hundreds of people. Glaciers in the Himalaya are retreating, sea levels are rising, and floods, droughts and cyclones are becoming more frequent and intense. Global warming is no longer a forecast; it is the reality of our times.

What is happening and why

Global warming is the long-term rise in the Earth's average surface temperature, caused mainly by human activities that release greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and gas, methane from agriculture, landfills and fossil fuel extraction, and nitrous oxide from fertilisers. These gases trap heat in the atmosphere like a blanket. Deforestation adds to the problem by removing the trees that absorb carbon dioxide. The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is now higher than at any time in at least two million years.

Climate change is the broader set of changes that follow: shifts in rainfall, more extreme weather, melting ice, rising and warming oceans, and changes in ecosystems. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has concluded that it is "unequivocal" that human influence has warmed the planet.

The impacts

  • Heat waves: more frequent and deadly, reducing labour productivity and harming health.
  • Water: erratic monsoons, melting glaciers and falling groundwater threaten water security for hundreds of millions.
  • Agriculture: heat and erratic rain reduce yields of wheat and rice; farmers face greater risk and debt.
  • Disasters: heavier rainfall causes floods and landslides; warmer seas fuel stronger cyclones.
  • Coasts: rising seas erode coastlines and push salt water into farmland in the Sundarbans and elsewhere.
  • Health: spread of vector-borne diseases like dengue and malaria; heat stress.
  • Biodiversity: coral reefs bleach; species are pushed to extinction.
  • Inequality: the poor, who contribute least to emissions, suffer most; climate change may push millions into poverty and migration.

The response

The world responded through the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992), the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement (2015), under which countries aim to limit warming to well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C. But current pledges still put the world on course for well over 2 °C of warming.

Mitigation — cutting emissions — requires a shift to renewable energy, energy efficiency, electric transport, sustainable agriculture and protection of forests. Adaptation — coping with unavoidable changes — requires drought-resistant crops, early warning systems, heat action plans, resilient infrastructure and water conservation.

India's role

India is the world's third-largest emitter in total, but its per-capita emissions are less than half the global average. It has pledged net zero by 2070, and in 2025 non-fossil sources crossed half of its installed power capacity. It leads the International Solar Alliance, runs a National Green Hydrogen Mission, and promotes Mission LiFE — a movement for sustainable lifestyles. India also insists on climate justice: developed countries, responsible for most past emissions, must lead in cutting emissions and provide finance and technology to developing countries.

What each of us can do

Individuals matter too: saving electricity, using public transport, reducing waste, eating sustainably, planting trees and supporting climate-friendly policies. Collective action begins with personal responsibility.

Conclusion

Climate change is the defining challenge of our century. It tests our science, our economies and above all our sense of responsibility towards the poor and towards future generations. As the saying goes, we do not inherit the Earth from our ancestors; we borrow it from our children. The technologies to solve the crisis exist and are becoming cheaper every year. What we need now is urgency, cooperation and justice — before the window to act closes.

What Lies Ahead for the Indian Economy?

India is today one of the world's fastest-growing large economies and among its five largest. It has a young population, a vibrant digital public infrastructure, a large domestic market and ambitious goals — to become a developed nation, "Viksit Bharat", by 2047. Yet it also faces deep challenges: creating jobs for millions of young people, raising incomes of farmers and informal workers, and growing sustainably in a world of climate change and geopolitical uncertainty. What lies ahead depends on how these opportunities and challenges are handled.

Strengths that point to a bright future

First, demography. About two-thirds of Indians are of working age, and this demographic window will remain open for about two more decades.

Second, digital public infrastructure. Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and the Account Aggregator framework have made payments, identity and data-sharing cheap and universal. UPI now handles billions of transactions every month, bringing millions into the formal economy.

Third, infrastructure investment. Public capital spending on highways, railways, ports, airports, power and urban transport has risen sharply, lowering logistics costs and attracting private investment.

Fourth, services strength. India is a global leader in IT services and global capability centres, and its services exports continue to grow.

Fifth, manufacturing push. Production Linked Incentive schemes have made India the second-largest mobile phone manufacturer, and companies seeking to diversify away from China are investing in electronics, pharmaceuticals and renewable equipment.

Sixth, macroeconomic stability. Banks have cleaned up their balance sheets, inflation is under control, and foreign exchange reserves are large.

Challenges ahead

  • Jobs: growth has not created enough good-quality jobs; many young people are underemployed, and women's participation in work is low.
  • Agriculture: nearly half the workforce depends on farming, which produces only about a sixth of output.
  • Human capital: learning levels, health and skills need major improvement.
  • Inequality: gains are concentrated among a few, and rural consumption lags.
  • Private investment has been slow to pick up.
  • Climate risks: heat waves, floods and droughts threaten agriculture, health and infrastructure.
  • Global uncertainty: trade wars, tariffs, wars and supply-chain disruptions.
  • Fiscal pressures: high public debt limits room for spending.

What should be done

  • Labour-intensive manufacturing — textiles, footwear, food processing, electronics assembly — to absorb workers moving out of agriculture.
  • Education and skilling reform focused on foundational learning and job-ready skills.
  • Agricultural reform: productivity, diversification, markets and climate resilience.
  • Ease of doing business: simpler regulations, faster courts, land and labour reforms at State level.
  • Women's participation: safety, childcare and flexible work.
  • Green growth: renewable energy, electric mobility and green hydrogen can become new engines of growth and jobs.
  • Trade integration: trade agreements to join global value chains.

Conclusion

The Indian economy stands at a turning point. If India uses its demographic dividend, digital strength and infrastructure push to build human capital and create jobs, it can become a developed nation within a generation. If it fails, growth may remain uneven and fragile. The future is not predetermined; it will be shaped by the choices of policymakers, businesses and citizens. With wise reforms and inclusive growth, what lies ahead can be India's most prosperous era.

In the post-Mauryan period (c. 200 BCE–300 CE), trade between India and the Roman Empire flourished, especially after the discovery of the monsoon winds (attributed to the Greek sailor Hippalus, 1st century BCE), which allowed ships to cross the Arabian Sea directly. Our sources include the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, Pliny's Natural History, Ptolemy's Geography, Sangam literature (which mentions the Yavanas) and archaeological finds of Roman coins and pottery.

1. Main ports

Arikamedu has yielded Roman amphorae, Arretine pottery and glass, showing a Roman trading station.

2. Internal trade routes

  • Uttarapatha: from Taxila through Mathura and Kaushambi to Pataliputra and Tamralipti — linked to the Silk Route through the Kushana empire.
  • Dakshinapatha: from Ujjain to Pratishthana (Paithan) and Tagara (Ter), bringing goods to Barygaza.
  • Routes across the Deccan to the east and west coasts under the Satavahanas; river routes on the Ganga.
  • Guilds (shrenis) organised production and trade; merchants donated to Buddhist caves along these routes (Karle, Nashik).

3. Commodities

4. Significance

  • Balance of trade favoured India: Pliny complained that India drained Rome of about 50 million sesterces a year.
  • Hoards of Roman coins in south India (Coimbatore, Madurai) and the use of gold coins by the Kushanas show the inflow of gold.
  • Prosperity of urban centres, guilds and Buddhist monasteries; spread of Indian culture abroad.
  • The trade declined in the 3rd century CE with the crisis of the Roman Empire.

1. Rise of the Bhakti Movement

  • It began in south India (6th–9th centuries) with the Tamil Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva), who sang in Tamil, opposed ritualism and welcomed all castes and women (Andal, Karaikkal Ammaiyar).
  • It was given a philosophical base by acharyas: Shankaracharya (Advaita, 8th century), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th–12th), Madhvacharya (Dvaita, 13th), Nimbarka and Vallabha.
  • It spread north from the 14th century: Ramananda, Kabir, Ravidas, Guru Nanak (nirguna), and Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Chaitanya (saguna); in Maharashtra Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram; in Karnataka the Virashaivas (Basavanna).

2. Nature of the movement

  • Devotion (bhakti) to a personal god as the path to salvation, more than rituals or knowledge.
  • Equality: rejection of caste and gender barriers; many saints came from lower castes.
  • Vernacular languages: Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi — creating rich literature.
  • Criticism of ritualism, idol worship (nirguna saints) and priestly control.
  • Synthesis with Sufism, promoting Hindu–Muslim harmony.

3. Advaita and Dvaita

  • Advaita gave a philosophical basis to nirguna bhakti — devotion to a formless God, as in Kabir.
  • Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita gave strong support to saguna bhakti — loving devotion to a personal God like Krishna or Rama; Madhva's ideas influenced the Haridasa movement in Karnataka and the Chaitanya tradition in Bengal.

The Bhakti movement thus combined deep philosophy with popular devotion and social reform, shaping Indian religion and culture for centuries.

Depletion of Natural Resources: A Threat to Humanity

Every year, a group of scientists calculates Earth Overshoot Day — the date by which humanity has used up all the natural resources that the planet can regenerate in that year. In recent years, it has fallen in late July or early August. For the rest of the year, we live on credit, drawing down forests, fisheries, soils, groundwater and the atmosphere's capacity to absorb carbon. Like a family that spends its savings instead of living on its income, humanity is heading towards bankruptcy — not financial, but ecological.

The scale of depletion

The UN Environment Programme's Global Resources Outlook (2024) reports that the extraction of materials — biomass, fossil fuels, metals and minerals — has more than tripled since 1970 and could rise by another 60% by 2060 if trends continue.

  • Water: groundwater is being pumped faster than it is recharged in India, the United States, China and the Middle East. Rivers like the Colorado and Yellow no longer reach the sea in some seasons; in India, cities like Chennai and Bengaluru have faced severe water crises.
  • Soil: erosion, salinity and loss of organic matter are degrading farmland; about 30% of India's land is degraded.
  • Forests: about ten million hectares are lost worldwide every year.
  • Fisheries: more than a third of the world's fish stocks are overfished.
  • Minerals and energy: oil, gas and high-grade ores are finite; even sand — used in concrete — is being mined so heavily that riverbeds and coasts are damaged.
  • Biodiversity: species are disappearing far faster than the natural rate.

Why depletion threatens humanity

First, food and water security. When aquifers run dry and soils lose fertility, harvests fall. The Green Revolution heartland of Punjab now faces a groundwater crisis.

Second, economic stability. Scarce resources mean rising prices, supply disruptions and slower growth; industries dependent on water, minerals and energy become vulnerable.

Third, conflict and migration. Competition over water, land and minerals fuels tensions within and between countries. Drought and land degradation push people to migrate.

Fourth, climate change. Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests release the greenhouse gases that are warming the planet, which in turn worsens water stress and crop losses.

Fifth, injustice. The poor, who depend directly on forests, fisheries and common lands, suffer first, while a wealthy minority consumes the most. Future generations will inherit a poorer planet — a deep injustice to those who have no voice today.

The causes

The root causes include population growth, rising consumption, especially by the rich, wasteful production, subsidies that encourage overuse (such as free electricity for pumping groundwater), poor regulation and an economic model that counts the use of natural capital as income.

What can be done

  • Efficiency: produce more with less — micro-irrigation, energy-efficient buildings and appliances, precision farming.
  • Circular economy: reduce, reuse, repair and recycle materials; extended producer responsibility for plastics, batteries and e-waste.
  • Renewables: shift from coal and oil to solar, wind and other clean sources.
  • Restoration: reforestation, watershed development, soil conservation and the revival of lakes and wetlands.
  • Pricing nature: remove harmful subsidies and account for natural capital in economic decisions.
  • Community management: local people can manage forests, fisheries and groundwater well, as India's Joint Forest Management and Atal Bhujal Yojana show.
  • Sustainable lifestyles: India's Mission LiFE asks individuals to consume mindfully and avoid waste.
  • Global cooperation on climate, oceans and biodiversity.

Conclusion

Mahatma Gandhi warned that the Earth provides enough for everyone's need but not for everyone's greed. The depletion of natural resources is not a distant problem; it is already shaping our water, food, climate and peace. Humanity has the knowledge and technology to live within the planet's limits. What it needs now is the will to change. The resources we save today are not merely ours; they belong to the generations yet to come.

Impact of Agricultural Reforms on India's Economic Future

Agriculture employs nearly half of India's workforce but produces only about a sixth of its national output. This gap explains much of rural distress: too many people depend on small, low-productivity farms. India's economic future — its growth, jobs, food security and social stability — therefore depends on reforming agriculture.

The need for reform

Indian farms are small (the average holding is just over one hectare), yields are below world averages, and much of the land depends on rain. Farmers face volatile prices, debt, weak access to markets and storage, and the growing effects of climate change. Public procurement at minimum support prices (MSP) mainly benefits rice and wheat farmers in a few States, encouraging water-intensive crops in water-scarce regions. The sector needs new investment, technology and markets.

The 2020 reforms and their fate

In 2020, Parliament passed three farm laws to allow farmers to sell outside regulated APMC mandis, to promote contract farming and to reduce stock limits under the Essential Commodities Act. Supporters argued that these would widen markets, attract private investment and raise farmers' incomes. But many farmers, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, feared the weakening of mandis and MSP, and that large companies would dominate. After a year-long protest, the laws were repealed in November 2021. The episode showed that reforms must be built through consultation and trust.

Reforms that are reshaping agriculture

Even without those laws, several reforms are changing the sector:

  • Income support: PM-KISAN gives ₹6,000 a year to farm families.
  • Markets: the e-NAM platform links mandis online; 10,000 Farmer Producer Organisations help small farmers bargain collectively.
  • Infrastructure: the ₹1 lakh crore Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for storage, cold chains and processing.
  • Digital agriculture: the Digital Agriculture Mission and Agri Stack aim to give farmers digital identities, crop surveys and advisories.
  • Risk cover: crop insurance under PMFBY and higher limits for Kisan Credit Cards.
  • Sustainability: natural farming, micro-irrigation, soil health cards and crop diversification towards pulses, oilseeds and millets.
  • Allied sectors: dairy, fisheries and poultry, which are growing faster than crops.

Impact on India's economic future

If carried through, these reforms can:

  • Raise farm incomes, increasing rural demand for industrial goods and services and supporting overall growth.
  • Create rural non-farm jobs in food processing, logistics and agri-tech, helping to move surplus labour out of farming.
  • Strengthen food and nutrition security while reducing the burden of food subsidies.
  • Boost exports — India is already the largest rice exporter and a major exporter of spices and marine products.
  • Reduce inflation volatility through better storage and supply chains.
  • Protect natural resources, making agriculture resilient to climate change.

Challenges

  • Small holdings and fragmented land records limit scale.
  • Political sensitivity of MSP, subsidies and markets.
  • State subject: agriculture and markets are largely State responsibilities, requiring Centre–State cooperation.
  • Climate risks — heat waves and erratic rain.
  • Skills and capital for farmers to use technology.

Conclusion

Agriculture is not a sector of the past; it is the foundation of India's future. Reforms that raise productivity, open markets fairly, protect farmers from risk and conserve soil and water can turn rural India into an engine of growth. The lesson of recent years is that reforms succeed only when farmers are partners, not mere subjects, of change. A prosperous farmer is the surest guarantee of a prosperous India.

The Mauryan period (c. 321–185 BCE) is one of the most important periods of Indian history for several reasons.

1. Political unification

  • Chandragupta Maurya, with Kautilya's help, overthrew the Nandas and built the first empire covering most of the subcontinent, from Afghanistan to Karnataka.
  • He defeated Seleucus Nicator, gaining territories in the north-west and a marriage alliance; Bindusara and Ashoka extended it further (Kalinga, c. 261 BCE).

2. Rich and varied sources

  • Kautilya's Arthashastra on statecraft and economy, Megasthenes' Indica (in fragments), the Ashokan edicts — the first deciphered written records of Indian rulers (read by James Prinsep in 1837) — and Buddhist and Jain texts.

3. Centralised administration

  • A council of ministers (mantriparishad), departments under adhyakshas, provinces under princes (kumaras), city administration at Pataliputra by committees (Megasthenes), a large standing army, and an efficient spy system.

4. Economy

  • State control of agriculture (sita land), mines, forests and trade; punch-marked silver coins; guilds; roads such as the Uttarapatha; growth of towns.

5. Ashoka and Dhamma

  • After Kalinga, Ashoka adopted Dhamma — tolerance, non-violence and welfare — and spread Buddhism to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and South-East Asia.

6. Art and architecture

  • The polished stone pillars with animal capitals — the Sarnath lion capital is India's national emblem; stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut in their early form); rock-cut Barabar caves; the Didarganj Yakshi.

7. International contacts

  • Diplomatic relations with the Hellenistic world; Ashoka's edicts mention Greek kings.

The Mauryan period thus marks the beginning of an imperial tradition, a written history and a pan-Indian culture, which is why it continues to attract historians.

The Chola Empire (c. 850–1279 CE), founded by Vijayalaya and raised to its height by Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044), was the greatest power of south India and controlled sea trade in the Bay of Bengal.

1. Administrative features

  • Monarchy with a council of officials; kings took titles like Rajakesari and Parakesari.
  • Units: the kingdom (rajyam) was divided into mandalams (provinces), valanadus, nadus and villages.
  • Local self-government — the most famous feature:

- Ur — assembly of ordinary villages; - Sabha (mahasabha) — assembly of Brahmana villages (brahmadeyas); - Nagaram — assembly of merchants. - The Uttaramerur inscriptions (919 and 921 CE, under Parantaka I) describe the election of committees by lot (kudavolai system), qualifications of members (property, education, age), and disqualifications. - Committees (variyams) looked after tanks, gardens, justice and temples.

  • Land revenue: Rajaraja ordered a land survey; revenue of about one-third of produce; tax in cash or kind.
  • Strong army and navy: Rajendra I's naval expedition to Srivijaya (1025) and conquests in Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his campaign to the Ganga gave him the title Gangaikondachola.
  • Irrigation: large tanks, such as the Cholagangam tank, and canals from the Kaveri.

2. Cultural features

  • Temple architecture (Dravida style): the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (1010) with its tall vimana; Gangaikondacholapuram and Airavatesvara (Darasuram) — together the Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO).
  • Bronze sculpture: the Nataraja and other bronzes made by the lost-wax process are among the finest in the world.
  • Literature: Tamil works such as Kamban's Ramayana, Sekkizhar's Periyapuranam on the Nayanars, and Jayankondar's Kalingattupparani; the compilation of the Shaiva canon (Tirumurai) and Vaishnava hymns.
  • Temples as centres of economy, education, music and dance; devadasis and temple endowments.
  • Bhakti movement of Alvars and Nayanars strengthened.
  • Overseas influence in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.

The Chola period is regarded as a golden age of Tamil culture and of local self-government in India.

Our Urban Survival Depends upon Efficient Waste Management

In March 2023, a fire at the Brahmapuram dumpsite in Kochi burned for nearly two weeks, covering the city in toxic smoke. Delhi's Ghazipur landfill has grown so high that it is jokingly compared to the Qutub Minar, and fires and collapses there have killed people. These are not isolated accidents. They are warnings that our cities are being buried under their own waste. As India urbanises rapidly, how we manage waste will decide whether our cities remain liveable.

The scale of the problem

Indian cities generate about 1.6 lakh tonnes of municipal solid waste every day, and the amount is rising with incomes and consumption. Though collection has improved greatly, a large share is still dumped without treatment in open landfills. Add to this sewage, plastic waste, construction and demolition debris, biomedical waste and fast-growing electronic waste, and the challenge becomes enormous. Most cities treat only a fraction of their sewage, which flows into rivers and lakes.

Why waste threatens urban survival

First, public health. Uncollected garbage breeds flies, mosquitoes and rats, spreading dengue, malaria, cholera and typhoid. Burning waste releases toxic dioxins and fine particles that worsen the air pollution that already shortens lives in Indian cities.

Second, water and soil pollution. Leachate from landfills seeps into groundwater, and untreated sewage turns rivers like the Yamuna into drains.

Third, urban flooding. Plastic bags and debris choke drains, so even moderate rain floods streets, as Mumbai, Chennai and Bengaluru have seen.

Fourth, climate change. Rotting organic waste in landfills produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and landfill fires add more emissions.

Fifth, loss of land and resources. Landfills occupy valuable land, and materials that could be recycled — plastic, metal, paper, organic matter — are wasted.

Finally, social injustice. Lakhs of waste-pickers, often women and children, work without protection or recognition, exposed to disease and danger.

Signs of hope

The Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban), launched in 2014, and its second phase from 2021 aim at garbage-free cities, segregation at source, scientific processing and the remediation of legacy dumpsites. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 and the Plastic Waste Management Rules with extended producer responsibility set clear duties for citizens, municipalities and producers. Indore, repeatedly ranked India's cleanest city in the Swachh Survekshan, shows what is possible: near-total segregation into wet and dry waste, door-to-door collection, composting, a bio-CNG plant that runs city buses, and the clearing of its old dumpsite. Cities such as Ambikapur have built models around women's self-help groups managing waste.

What efficient waste management requires

  • Segregation at source: households and businesses must separate wet, dry and hazardous waste — the foundation of everything else.
  • Reduce and reuse: cutting single-use plastics, encouraging refill and repair, and the "LiFE" lifestyle.
  • Decentralised processing: composting and biogas at the level of homes, colonies and markets.
  • Recycling and the circular economy: material recovery facilities, waste-to-wealth enterprises and extended producer responsibility.
  • Integrating waste-pickers into the formal system with identity cards, safety gear and fair pay.
  • Scientific landfills only for inert residue, and biomining of old dumpsites.
  • Sewage treatment and reuse of treated water.
  • Financing and governance: user charges, capable municipal bodies and public–private partnerships.
  • Citizen behaviour: awareness, penalties for littering and community ownership.

Conclusion

A city is like a living body: if it cannot get rid of its waste, it sickens and dies. Our urban future depends not only on metro lines and flyovers but on what happens to the garbage we throw away each morning. If we treat waste as a resource rather than a nuisance, we can make our cities cleaner, healthier and more sustainable. Efficient waste management is not a municipal chore; it is a condition of urban survival.

Paradox of Freedom and Responsibility

Freedom is the most cherished of human values. Revolutions have been fought for it, and constitutions are written to protect it. Yet the more freedom we have, the more responsibility we must carry. This is the paradox: freedom seems to mean doing what we like, but true freedom can survive only when it is limited by responsibility.

The meaning of freedom

Freedom has two faces. Negative freedom is freedom from interference — no one should stop me from speaking, believing or moving. Positive freedom is freedom to — the ability to shape one's own life, which needs education, health and opportunity. Both are precious. India's Constitution guarantees freedom of speech, movement, religion and occupation, and the Supreme Court has expanded the right to life and personal liberty to include dignity and privacy.

Why freedom needs responsibility

First, my freedom ends where another's begins. John Stuart Mill's harm principle holds that people may do as they wish so long as they do not harm others. Freedom of speech does not include the freedom to spread hatred or false rumours that incite violence. That is why Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions in the interests of public order, decency and the rights of others.

Second, freedom without responsibility destroys itself. If every driver ignored traffic rules in the name of freedom, no one would be able to drive safely. If citizens refused to pay taxes or obey laws, the State that protects their liberty would collapse. Anarchy leads not to freedom but to the rule of the strongest.

Third, freedom brings the burden of choice. The philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre said that human beings are "condemned to be free": since we choose our actions, we are responsible for them and cannot blame fate or others. The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who survived Nazi concentration camps, once suggested that America's Statue of Liberty on the East Coast should be balanced by a Statue of Responsibility on the West Coast.

The paradox in modern life

Social media has given every person a megaphone. This has empowered ordinary citizens to expose injustice and share ideas. But the same freedom has spread fake news, cyberbullying and hate, sometimes leading to mob violence. Technology companies enjoy freedom to innovate, but they must take responsibility for privacy and the harm caused by their platforms. Economic freedom has created wealth, but without responsibility towards workers and the environment, it has also caused inequality and pollution. Even personal freedom — to eat, drink or travel as we like — affects public health and the planet.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the paradox became visible to all. The freedom to move about and gather had to be balanced against the responsibility to protect the vulnerable from infection.

The Indian view

Indian thought has long linked rights with duties. The idea of dharma stresses duty to family, society and nature. Mahatma Gandhi argued that rights flow from duties well performed. The Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), added by the 42nd Amendment, remind citizens to respect the Constitution, promote harmony, protect the environment and develop a scientific temper.

Resolving the paradox

The paradox dissolves when we see freedom and responsibility not as opposites but as two sides of the same coin. Responsibility is the price of freedom, and freedom is the reward of responsibility. Children are given more freedom as they show more responsibility; nations that act responsibly earn the trust and freedom of the international community. A free press remains free when it is responsible; a free market stays free when it is fair.

This requires:

  • Education that teaches critical thinking and ethics, not merely rights;
  • Laws that protect liberty while restraining harm;
  • Institutions that hold the powerful accountable;
  • Personal self-discipline — what Indian philosophy calls atma-sanyam.

Conclusion

Freedom is not a licence to do anything; it is the opportunity to do what is right. As citizens of a democracy, we are free because we accept the responsibility of respecting the freedom of others. The true test of a free society is not how much people can do as they please, but how willingly they choose to do what is just.

From the early centuries CE, Indian merchants, Brahmanas and Buddhist monks travelled to Suvarnabhumi (South-East Asia). Their influence spread mainly through trade and voluntary cultural exchange, not conquest, and local rulers adopted Indian ideas to strengthen their kingship.

1. Indianised kingdoms

  • Funan (lower Mekong, 1st–6th century): legend says it was founded by a Brahmana, Kaundinya, who married a local Naga princess.
  • Champa (central Vietnam): Sanskrit inscriptions and the Shaiva temple complex of My Son.
  • Kambuja (Khmer Empire, Cambodia): Jayavarman II (802 CE) began the devaraja cult; Angkor Wat, built by Suryavarman II in the 12th century as a Vishnu temple, is the largest religious monument in the world; Angkor Thom and the Bayon of Jayavarman VII are Buddhist.
  • Dvaravati (Mon, Thailand), Pyu and Pagan (Myanmar — Ananda temple), and Vat Phou in Laos.

2. Religion

  • Shaivism and Vaishnavism under royal patronage; temples of Shiva and Vishnu.
  • Mahayana, and later Theravada Buddhism (via Sri Lanka), which remains the main religion of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.

3. Language and script

  • Sanskrit was the language of royal inscriptions (the Vo Canh inscription in Vietnam is among the oldest).
  • The Pallava Grantha script of south India gave rise to the Khmer, Thai, Lao, Burmese and Mon scripts.
  • Thai and Khmer have many Sanskrit and Pali words (for example Rama, Siam, Ayutthaya from Ayodhya).

4. Literature and performing arts

  • The Ramayana became part of local culture: Reamker (Cambodia), Ramakien (Thailand), Phra Lak Phra Lam (Laos); Thai kings took the title Rama.
  • The Mahabharata, Jataka tales and Puranic stories appear in sculpture and shadow plays; classical dances drew on Indian forms.

5. Polity, law and architecture

  • Ideas of kingship, the Manusmriti-based law codes, the use of Brahmana priests in court rituals (the Thai royal court still keeps them).
  • Temple architecture inspired by Indian styles, adapted to local forms.

Assessment: Indian culture was adapted, not imposed — local traditions blended with Indian ideas. Today the shared heritage supports India's Act East Policy: the Archaeological Survey of India has helped restore Angkor Wat, Ta Prohm, My Son and Vat Phou, and the Mekong–Ganga Cooperation (2000) builds on these links.

Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540–1545) ruled for only five years, but he is remembered both as a great general and as one of medieval India's finest administrators.

1. Military genius — comparable to Babur

  • Defeated Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj/Bilgram (1540), driving the Mughals out of India.
  • Brilliant use of strategy, surprise and diplomacy: he took the Rohtas fort by a ruse and timed the Chausa attack for when Humayun's camp was unprepared.
  • Conquered Malwa, Raisen, Multan, Sindh and fought the Rajputs of Marwar at Sammel (1544), a hard-won victory after which he remarked that he had nearly lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet.
  • Died at Kalinjar (1545) while besieging it.
  • Army reforms: a large standing army under his direct control; dagh (branding of horses) and huliya (descriptive rolls of soldiers) to stop fraud, following Alauddin Khalji.

Like Babur (Panipat 1526, Khanwa 1527, Ghaghra 1529), he was a master of battlefield tactics; but his success came mostly through planning and diplomacy rather than new weapons such as Babur's artillery.

2. Administrative genius — forerunner of Akbar

  • Provincial structure: empire divided into sarkars and parganas, with officials like the shiqdar-i-shiqdaran (law and order) and munshif-i-munshifan (revenue and justice).
  • Land revenue: measurement of land with the jarib; crop rates (rai); the state's share fixed at one-third of produce; patta (title deed) and qabuliyat (agreement) given to peasants; relief for crop failure.
  • Currency: the silver rupiya (about 178 grains) and copper dam — the basis of later currency.
  • Communication and trade: the Sarak-i-Azam (Grand Trunk Road) from Sonargaon to Peshawar, and other roads; sarais along roads that served as dak (postal) stations and markets; abolition of internal customs duties.
  • Law and order: village headmen (muqaddams) held responsible for crimes in their area.
  • Justice: strict and impartial.

3. Comparison with Akbar

Raja Todar Mal, who served Sher Shah, later framed Akbar's revenue system. Akbar's administration thus built on Sher Shah's foundations.

Conclusion: although his reign was brief and his dynasty ended soon after, Sher Shah's achievements in war and administration justify comparisons with both Babur and Akbar. His tomb at Sasaram is a reminder of his greatness.

Ethical Dilemmas and Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into everyday life. It recommends what we watch, screens our job applications, reads our X-rays, translates our languages and, through tools such as ChatGPT, even writes essays like this one. AI promises enormous benefits — faster diagnosis of disease, better weather forecasts, personalised education and higher productivity. But because AI systems make or shape decisions that affect human lives, they raise difficult ethical dilemmas: questions of fairness, responsibility, privacy, truth and control.

Bias and fairness

AI learns from data, and data reflects the prejudices of the society that produced it. A recruitment algorithm trained on past hiring data may learn to prefer men; facial recognition systems have been found to be less accurate for women and people with darker skin; risk-assessment software used in some American courts was accused of rating Black defendants as more likely to reoffend. In a country as diverse as India, an AI system trained mostly on English-speaking urban users may misunderstand or exclude rural people, women and speakers of other languages. The dilemma is that AI can make decisions appear objective while hiding discrimination inside a "black box".

Accountability and transparency

When a self-driving car causes an accident, or an AI system denies a loan or a medical treatment, who is responsible — the programmer, the company, the user or the machine? Many advanced AI models are so complex that even their designers cannot fully explain their decisions. Yet people have a right to know why a decision affecting them was made and to challenge it. The classic "trolley problem" — whether a self-driving car should protect its passengers or pedestrians — shows how engineers are now forced to encode moral choices into machines.

Privacy and surveillance

AI feeds on data. Facial recognition in public places, predictive policing and the profiling of consumers can turn societies into surveillance states. Personal data may be collected without meaningful consent and used to manipulate opinions and behaviour, as the Cambridge Analytica scandal showed.

Truth, deepfakes and democracy

Generative AI can produce realistic fake images, voices and videos. Deepfakes have been used to spread misinformation, defame individuals — often women — and commit fraud by imitating a relative's voice. In an age when anyone can create convincing falsehoods, trust in information and in democratic debate is threatened.

Work and inequality

AI can automate routine jobs in offices, call centres and factories. While it will also create new jobs, the transition may leave many workers behind and concentrate wealth in a few technology companies and countries. Should those who profit from automation share the gains with those who lose their jobs?

Autonomy and lethal weapons

Perhaps the gravest dilemma is the use of AI in warfare. Autonomous weapons that can select and kill targets without human intervention raise the question of whether a machine should ever decide to take a human life. There are also concerns about AI systems becoming so powerful that humans lose meaningful control over them.

Towards ethical AI

These dilemmas do not mean we should reject AI. They mean we must shape it. Several principles are now widely accepted:

  • Fairness: test systems for bias and use diverse data.
  • Transparency and explainability: people should know when they are dealing with AI and why it decided as it did.
  • Accountability: clear legal responsibility for harm.
  • Privacy: data protection laws such as India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
  • Human oversight: humans must remain "in the loop" for high-stakes decisions.
  • Safety and security testing before deployment.

The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) and the European Union's AI Act (2024), which bans some uses and strictly regulates high-risk ones, are steps in this direction. India's IndiaAI Mission emphasises "AI for All" and responsible, inclusive AI, and India has led global discussions on AI governance. Companies too must build ethics into design, not add it as an afterthought.

Conclusion

AI is a mirror and a magnifier: it reflects our values and multiplies their effects. Whether it becomes a tool for justice and prosperity or for discrimination and control depends not on the machine but on us. The central ethical task of our time is to ensure that intelligent machines remain servants of human dignity, and that in the race to make machines smarter, we do not make humans less free.

The Revival of Traditional Indian Sports

Long before cricket and football arrived in India, children in its villages ran, wrestled, chased and climbed in games passed down through generations. Kabaddi, kho-kho, gilli-danda, mallakhamb, kalaripayattu, wrestling in the akhada, boat races in Kerala and archery in the North-East were part of the country's culture. Chess itself grew out of the ancient Indian game of chaturanga. For decades, these sports were neglected, seen as rustic pastimes rather than serious sport. Today they are enjoying a remarkable revival.

Signs of revival

The most striking example is kabaddi. The Pro Kabaddi League, launched in 2014, turned a village game into a television spectacle watched by crores of people, with professional players, sponsors and international stars. India has dominated kabaddi at the Asian Games and in World Cups.

Kho-kho has followed. A professional league, Ultimate Kho Kho, began in 2022, and India hosted the first Kho Kho World Cup in New Delhi in January 2025, with Indian teams winning both the men's and women's titles.

The government's Khelo India programme has included indigenous sports such as gatka, kalaripayattu, thang-ta and mallakhamb in the Khelo India Youth Games, and yogasana has been recognised as a competitive sport. Mallakhamb, the gymnastic art performed on a wooden pole, has spread to dozens of countries. Martial arts such as kalaripayattu and silambam attract learners worldwide, and traditional boat races, bull races and rural games draw large crowds at festivals.

Why revival matters

First, cultural heritage. Traditional sports carry local stories, music, festivals and values. Reviving them keeps alive a living heritage and strengthens community identity.

Second, accessible fitness. Most indigenous games need little or no equipment and can be played in any open space. In an age of sedentary lifestyles, obesity and screen addiction among children, they offer cheap, enjoyable exercise for all.

Third, inclusion. Rural youth, girls and people from poor families, who cannot afford expensive equipment and coaching, can excel in these sports. Many kabaddi and kho-kho stars come from small towns and farming families.

Fourth, values and skills. Games like kho-kho and kabaddi build speed, strategy, teamwork and quick decision-making; martial arts teach discipline and self-control.

Fifth, economic opportunity. Leagues, broadcasting, tourism and equipment create jobs and incomes; traditional sports can become part of India's soft power, much as yoga has.

Challenges

  • Lack of infrastructure, coaching and scientific training in rural areas.
  • Weak federations and poor governance in some sports.
  • Limited international recognition, which keeps these sports out of the Olympics and reduces funding.
  • Dominance of cricket in media attention and sponsorship.
  • Lack of documentation of many folk games, which are disappearing with urbanisation.

The way forward

  • Include traditional games in school physical education and inter-school competitions.
  • Standardise rules and build professional federations that can promote them internationally, as was done with kabaddi.
  • Use leagues and digital media to build fan bases.
  • Provide scholarships, jobs and recognition to players under schemes like Khelo India and the Target Olympic Podium Scheme, and in government service.
  • Document and revive dying folk games through cultural ministries and local communities.
  • Promote them through tourism and festivals.

Conclusion

The revival of traditional sports is not about turning back the clock or rejecting modern games. It is about recognising that India's own sporting heritage can produce champions, healthier citizens and pride in local culture. When a girl from a village wins a kho-kho world title, or a kabaddi raider from a farming family becomes a household name, India discovers that the playgrounds of its villages hold treasures worth preserving. As the nation dreams of becoming a sporting power, its roots can give it strength.

The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilization (c. 2600–1900 BCE, mature phase) built some of the earliest planned towns in the world — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi and Banawali.

Main features of Harappan townships

1. Planned layout

  • Streets cut each other at right angles, dividing the town into rectangular blocks (grid pattern).
  • Main streets were wide (up to 10 m at Mohenjo-daro) and ran north–south and east–west.

2. Division of the town

  • A raised, fortified citadel on the west for public buildings and the elite; a larger lower town on the east for residences.
  • Dholavira had three parts — citadel, middle town and lower town.

3. Burnt-brick construction

  • Standardised baked bricks in the ratio 1:2:4, used across the whole civilization.

4. Drainage and sanitation

  • Covered drains along streets with manholes; house drains joined street drains — a remarkable civic sense.
  • Bathrooms and wells in many houses; Mohenjo-daro had about 700 wells.

5. Public buildings

  • Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro — waterproofed with bitumen, probably for ritual bathing.
  • Granaries at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; an assembly hall.
  • Dockyard at Lothal for maritime trade.

6. Houses

  • One- or two-storey houses around a courtyard; doors opened into side lanes, not main streets, for privacy.

7. Water management

  • Dholavira had large reservoirs and channels to harvest rainwater in a dry region.

8. Uniformity

  • Standard weights (binary system), seals and bricks suggest a strong civic authority.

Significance: such town planning reflects a well-organised administration, trade and civic life, and has no parallel in contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia in sanitation. Dholavira became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

The Upanishads (c. 800–500 BCE) are the last part of the Vedic literature — hence Vedanta. They grew out of the Vedic tradition but shifted its focus so much that they are often seen as different in essence.

1. How they differ from earlier Vedic literature

  • Brahman and Atman: the central idea that the individual self (Atman) is identical with the universal reality (Brahman) — "Tat tvam asi" (Chandogya) and "Aham Brahmasmi" (Brihadaranyaka).
  • Criticism of ritual: the Mundaka Upanishad calls sacrifices "unsafe boats" for crossing the ocean of rebirth.
  • Karma, samsara and moksha appear clearly for the first time.
  • Dialogue and inquiry: teachings through questions — Yajnavalkya and Gargi, Nachiketa and Yama.
  • Ethics: self-control, truth and compassion over ritual purity.

2. Continuity with the Vedas

  • They are part of the Vedic corpus and use its language and symbols (Om, Gayatri).
  • Some earlier hymns, such as the Nasadiya Sukta, already asked philosophical questions.
  • They reinterpret the sacrifice as an inner, symbolic act rather than rejecting it entirely.

3. Significance

The Upanishads laid the basis of Vedanta, influenced Buddhism and Jainism, Shankaracharya and later thinkers such as Vivekananda and Gandhi. So they were different in emphasis and spirit, though not a complete break from the Vedic tradition.

Biodiversity and Human Existence

Every breath we take, every meal we eat and almost every medicine we use comes to us from the web of life. Bees pollinate our crops, microbes make our soils fertile, forests and oceans absorb the carbon we emit, and wetlands clean our water. Biodiversity — the variety of genes, species and ecosystems on Earth — is not a luxury to be admired in zoos and documentaries. It is the foundation of human existence. Yet we are destroying it at a speed never seen in human history.

What biodiversity gives us

Scientists call the benefits of nature ecosystem services. Provisioning services give us food, timber, fibre, fuel and fresh water. Nearly all our crops and livestock were domesticated from wild species, and their wild relatives still hold the genes we need to breed varieties that resist heat, drought and disease. Regulating services control climate, floods, pests and diseases: mangroves blunt cyclones, forests regulate rainfall, and predators keep pests in check. About three-quarters of the world's food crop types depend at least partly on animal pollinators. Supporting services such as soil formation and nutrient cycling make all life possible. Cultural services — the sacred groves of the Western Ghats and Meghalaya, the reverence for the tiger and the peepal tree, the joy of a bird's song — give meaning to human life.

Biodiversity is also a pharmacy. Aspirin came from willow bark, the anti-malarial artemisinin from a plant, and many cancer drugs from forest and marine organisms. Traditional systems such as Ayurveda and the knowledge of tribal healers rely on thousands of medicinal plants.

A crisis of our making

The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) warned in 2019 that about one million species face extinction. The WWF's Living Planet Report 2024 found that monitored wildlife populations have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. Many scientists speak of a sixth mass extinction, the first caused by a single species.

The drivers are well known: land-use change as forests and grasslands become farms, mines and cities; over-exploitation through overfishing, poaching and logging; climate change, which bleaches coral reefs and pushes species uphill; pollution by plastics, pesticides and fertilisers; and invasive species such as Lantana in Indian forests.

Why the loss threatens us

When biodiversity declines, ecosystems become fragile. A forest with fewer species is more vulnerable to pests and fire; a farm landscape without pollinators produces less food. The loss of natural habitat brings humans into closer contact with wildlife and raises the risk of diseases that jump from animals to people — COVID-19, Nipah and Ebola remind us of this danger. Fisheries collapse when oceans are overfished, threatening the protein supply of millions. Poor and indigenous communities, who depend most directly on nature, suffer first and most.

India's responsibility

India is one of the world's megadiverse countries, holding about 7–8% of recorded species on 2.4% of the world's land, and parts of four of the 36 global biodiversity hotspots — the Himalaya, the Western Ghats, the Indo-Burma region and Sundaland. Project Tiger has more than doubled the tiger population since 2006; the Asiatic lion has recovered in Gir; community efforts by the Bishnois and the Chipko movement are celebrated around the world. But wetlands are shrinking, grasslands are neglected, and species such as the Great Indian Bustard are close to extinction.

What must be done

The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) commits countries to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030 and to restore degraded ecosystems. India has updated its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan and amended the Biological Diversity Act in 2023. Real progress requires:

  • protecting and connecting habitats through corridors;
  • respecting the rights and knowledge of indigenous and local communities, who are often the best conservators;
  • sustainable agriculture and fisheries that work with nature;
  • fair sharing of benefits from the use of genetic resources;
  • valuing nature in economic decisions, and reducing wasteful consumption, as the Mission LiFE campaign urges.

Conclusion

Chief Seattle is often quoted as saying that man did not weave the web of life; he is merely a strand in it, and whatever he does to the web he does to himself. Biodiversity is not something separate from us that we can choose to save or spend. It is the living system that sustains us. To protect it is not charity towards other species — it is the condition for our own survival.

Data Privacy in the Digital Age

Every time we unlock a phone, pay through UPI, search the internet or walk past a CCTV camera, we leave a trail of data. That data reveals where we go, what we buy, whom we talk to, what we believe and even how we feel. In the digital age, data has been called the new oil. But unlike oil, data is about people. Who controls it, and how it is used, has become one of the central questions of freedom in our time.

Why privacy matters

Privacy is not about having something to hide. It is about autonomy and dignity — the freedom to think, communicate and live without being watched, profiled or manipulated. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21, including informational privacy.

Without privacy, democracy itself is at risk. The Cambridge Analytica scandal of 2018 showed how personal data of millions of Facebook users could be harvested to target political messages. Targeted advertising, credit scoring by algorithms and facial recognition can lead to discrimination, manipulation and surveillance.

The threats

  • Data breaches and cybercrime: hospitals, government portals and companies have suffered breaches; the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi in 2022 crippled its systems. Leaked data feeds fraud and identity theft.
  • Surveillance capitalism: many "free" apps earn money by collecting and selling behavioural data, often without meaningful consent.
  • State surveillance: powerful tools such as spyware can be misused against journalists, activists and opponents.
  • Artificial intelligence: AI systems are trained on huge datasets, including personal data, and deepfakes can misuse a person's face and voice.
  • Children are especially vulnerable to tracking and exploitation online.

India's legal response

After years of debate, India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It requires consent for processing personal data, limits use to specified purposes, gives citizens rights to access, correct and erase their data and to nominate someone, requires verifiable parental consent for children, and sets up a Data Protection Board that can impose penalties of up to ₹250 crore. The DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, with obligations coming into force in phases over 18 months.

Critics point out that the Act gives the government wide powers to exempt its own agencies, and that amendments to the RTI Act could restrict access to information. Supporters argue that it balances privacy with innovation and the needs of a digital economy. Its success will depend on how independently the Board functions and how seriously companies comply.

Building a privacy culture

Laws are necessary but not enough. We need:

  • Privacy by design: systems that collect only the data they need and protect it with encryption;
  • Strong cyber security for government and private databases;
  • Clear, simple consent instead of long, unreadable terms and conditions;
  • Digital literacy, so that citizens know their rights and can protect themselves from fraud;
  • Oversight of surveillance by Parliament and the courts;
  • Ethical AI, with transparency about how personal data is used.

India's digital public infrastructure, such as Aadhaar, UPI and the Account Aggregator framework, can show the world how to combine scale with consent-based data sharing — if privacy is built into its foundations.

Conclusion

Technology has given us immense convenience and opportunity, but it must remain our servant and not become our master. A digital society that does not respect privacy can slide into a surveillance society. The challenge of our age is to enjoy the benefits of data while ensuring that every person remains the owner of their own life story. As the Supreme Court reminded us, privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity.

After the Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE), whose bloodshed he regretted in Major Rock Edict XIII, Ashoka replaced bherighosha (the sound of war drums) with dhammaghosha (the sound of Dhamma). His Dhamma was not the Buddhist creed as such but a code of moral conduct and social responsibility meant for all his subjects.

1. Main principles of Ashoka's Dhamma

  • Respect and kindness: obedience to parents and elders, respect for teachers, kindness to slaves and servants, generosity to Brahmanas and Shramanas.
  • Non-violence: restrictions on animal slaughter and a ban on sacrifices and festive gatherings (samajas) involving killing (Rock Edict I); the royal kitchen cut meat dishes.
  • Tolerance (Rock Edict XII): honour all sects; restraint in speech (vachaguti); one who disparages others' sects harms his own.
  • Self-examination: avoid anger, cruelty, pride and envy.
  • Welfare (Rock Edict II, Pillar Edict VII): medical care for humans and animals, wells, rest houses and shade trees along roads.

2. How it was practised

  • Dhamma mahamattas (from the 13th regnal year, Rock Edict V) to spread Dhamma and look after the welfare of all sects, women and prisoners.
  • Dhamma yatras replaced royal hunting tours; the king met people and officials.
  • Rajukas and yuktas toured every five years to teach Dhamma and give justice.
  • Edicts in Prakrit in Brahmi and Kharosthi (and Greek and Aramaic in the north-west) so that ordinary people could understand them.
  • Missions abroad to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitra) and to Hellenistic kingdoms.
  • Lenient justice: a three-day respite for those sentenced to death.

3. Significance

Dhamma gave a common ethical bond to a vast, diverse empire and is an early example of a welfare state and of religious tolerance. Critics (H.C. Raychaudhuri) argue that the stress on non-violence weakened the army and contributed to the decline of the empire, while Romila Thapar sees it as a practical policy to unify the empire.

  • Patron of learning: he gave large grants to Nalanda, which Hiuen Tsang described as a great centre with thousands of students.

Decreasing Forest Cover and its Impact on the Human Race

Long before cities and farms, humanity was born in the forest. Forests gave our ancestors food, shelter, medicine and fuel, and they still give every one of us the air we breathe and much of the water we drink. Yet the world continues to lose them. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, about ten million hectares of forest are cut down every year — an area roughly the size of South Korea. In 2024 alone, fires and clearing destroyed a record area of tropical primary forest. The loss of forests is not only an environmental tragedy; it is a threat to the survival and well-being of the human race.

Why forests are disappearing

The main driver is the expansion of agriculture — cattle ranching and soya in the Amazon, oil palm in Indonesia and Malaysia, and shifting cultivation and encroachment elsewhere. Logging, mining, roads, dams and urban sprawl cut forests into fragments. Forest fires, made worse by heat and drought, now burn vast areas from Canada to Australia. Poverty, weak land rights and demand for cheap commodities in distant markets drive much of this destruction.

What the loss means for humanity

First, climate change. Forests store more carbon than the entire atmosphere. Deforestation releases this carbon and removes a sink that absorbs about a fifth to a quarter of the carbon dioxide we emit. Parts of the Amazon are close to a tipping point at which rainforest may turn into savanna and become a carbon source.

Second, water security. Forests regulate rainfall and river flow, recharge groundwater and protect catchments. When the hills are bare, rivers flood in the monsoon and run dry in summer. Mumbai's water comes from forested catchments; the Himalayan forests feed the rivers of the north Indian plains.

Third, disasters. Without tree roots, slopes slide and soils wash away. The landslides of Wayanad and the Himalaya, and the floods of Kerala, have been linked to the loss of forest and unplanned construction on fragile slopes. Mangroves protect coasts from cyclones and storm surges, as the Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika have shown.

Fourth, health. Clearing forests brings people and wildlife into closer contact and raises the risk of diseases that jump from animals to humans, such as Nipah and Ebola. Forests are also the source of many medicines, and smoke from forest fires kills thousands every year.

Fifth, livelihoods and culture. About 1.6 billion people worldwide, and an estimated 27 crore in India, depend on forests for food, fuel, fodder and income. For tribal communities, the forest is home, identity and the sacred. Their displacement is a human loss as well as an ecological one.

Finally, biodiversity. Forests hold most of the world's land species. The loss of pollinators, soil organisms and wild crop relatives threatens food security for all of us.

India's experience

India is one of the few countries where forest and tree cover has increased — to about a quarter of its area according to the India State of Forest Report 2023 — thanks to plantations, community efforts and agroforestry. Yet the quality of natural forests is a concern: dense forests are being degraded, the north-eastern States have lost cover, and plantations of a single species cannot replace natural forests rich in life. Large projects continue to divert forest land.

The way forward

  • Stop deforestation through strong laws, satellite monitoring and deforestation-free supply chains.
  • Secure the rights of forest communities, who are the best guardians of forests, under laws such as the Forest Rights Act.
  • Restore degraded land with native species: India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030.
  • Pay for ecosystem services, as India's Finance Commission does by giving weight to forest cover in sharing taxes with States.
  • Reduce consumption of products linked to deforestation, in the spirit of Mission LiFE.
  • Agroforestry and urban forests to meet timber needs and cool cities.

Conclusion

A Chinese proverb says that the best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago; the second-best time is now. The fate of forests and the fate of humanity are tied together. If we destroy forests, we destroy our own life-support system. If we protect and restore them, they will continue to give us air, water, food and stability for generations to come.

Need for Multidisciplinarity in Higher Education

The great problems of our time — climate change, pandemics, artificial intelligence, inequality — do not respect the walls between university departments. A climate scientist needs economics, an engineer designing AI needs ethics, and a doctor tackling a pandemic needs sociology and communication. Yet for decades Indian higher education has divided students early into rigid streams — science, commerce, arts — and kept them there. The need of the hour is multidisciplinarity.

What multidisciplinarity means

Multidisciplinary education allows students to study across fields: a physics student may take music, an engineering student philosophy, a history student data science. It also means research that brings different disciplines together to solve real problems. It is not new to India: ancient universities such as Takshashila and Nalanda taught grammar, medicine, logic, astronomy and the arts together, and the idea of the "64 kalas" combined many skills.

Why it is needed

First, complex problems need many lenses. Public health, sustainable cities and water management require science, technology, economics and social understanding together.

Second, the job market is changing. Automation is replacing routine tasks; employers value problem-solving, creativity, communication and the ability to learn new skills. A broad education prepares graduates for jobs that do not yet exist.

Third, innovation happens at the boundaries. Biotechnology, nanotechnology, behavioural economics and cognitive science were born when disciplines met.

Fourth, education for citizenship and character. The humanities and social sciences develop ethical reasoning, empathy and democratic values — essential when technology raises new moral questions.

Fifth, student choice and well-being. Rigid streams force teenagers to choose too early; flexibility lets them follow their interests and change course.

India's policy response

The National Education Policy 2020 makes multidisciplinarity central. It proposes large multidisciplinary universities and colleges, flexible four-year undergraduate programmes with multiple entry and exit options, an Academic Bank of Credits, and Multidisciplinary Education and Research Universities. The UGC's curriculum framework now allows students to combine major and minor subjects from different streams. IITs have added humanities and design departments; some new private universities follow the liberal-arts model.

Challenges

  • Faculty and infrastructure: most colleges are small and single-stream; affiliated colleges lack teachers in many subjects.
  • Mindsets: parents and students still value professional degrees and rank-based entrance examinations.
  • Assessment and recruitment: examinations and job criteria often reward narrow specialisation.
  • Risk of superficiality: breadth must not come at the cost of depth.
  • Funding: India spends far less on higher education and research than leading countries.

What should be done

  • Cluster small colleges into multidisciplinary institutions and allow credit transfer between them.
  • Train teachers for interdisciplinary teaching and support joint research centres.
  • Use online platforms such as SWAYAM to give students access to courses not available locally.
  • Reform entrance tests and recruitment to value broad learning.
  • Keep a balance: a strong major subject, with chosen minors and skills.

Conclusion

Rabindranath Tagore's Visva-Bharati sought an education in which art, science and life were one. In a world of rapid change, the most valuable graduates will be those who can connect ideas across fields and apply them with judgement and compassion. Multidisciplinarity is not a luxury but a necessity if Indian higher education is to produce thinkers, innovators and responsible citizens for a developed India.

Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE) built the Gupta Empire into the leading power of India. Most of what we know comes from the Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar inscription composed by his court poet Harisena, and from his coins.

1. As a statesman

  • Aryavarta (north India): he "uprooted" nine kings and annexed their lands — direct rule over the Ganga valley.
  • Dakshinapatha (south): he defeated twelve rulers, including Vishnugopa of Kanchi, but restored them as tributaries — the policy of grahana-moksha-anugraha (capture, release and favour). This avoided overstretching the empire.
  • Forest kingdoms (atavika rajyas) of central India were made his servants, securing the route south.
  • Frontier states (Samatata, Kamarupa, Nepal) and tribal republics (Malavas, Yaudheyas) paid tribute.
  • Distant rulers such as the Kushana "Daivaputra Shahi Shahanushahi", the Shakas and the king of Simhala sent embassies and gifts.
  • He performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and issued Ashvamedha coins to proclaim paramountcy.

V.A. Smith called him the "Indian Napoleon"; unlike Napoleon, he knew where to stop and used diplomacy.

2. As an administrator

  • A centralised core with a feudatory ring outside — a flexible model later Indian empires used.
  • Officials such as mahadandanayaka, sandhivigrahika (minister of war and peace — Harisena held this post) and kumaramatya.
  • Gold coins (dinaras) of fine quality showing prosperity; the "lyrist" type shows him playing the veena.
  • Patron of culture: a poet himself (Kaviraja), patron of Sanskrit learning; he followed Vaishnavism yet tolerated Buddhism (he allowed the king of Sri Lanka to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya).

3. Critical evaluation

  • The inscription is a court eulogy and exaggerates; little is known of his civil administration.
  • The southern "conquest" was a raid more than lasting rule.

Still, Samudragupta combined military skill with realistic statecraft and laid the foundation of the Gupta "classical age".

Shramana traditionAhimsaKarmaRejection of Vedic ritual

Gautama Buddha and Vardhamana Mahavira were contemporaries of the 6th–5th century BCE who belonged to the shramana (ascetic) tradition that questioned Brahmanical orthodoxy.

Similarities in their teachings

  • Rejection of Vedic authority and ritual: both denied that animal sacrifices and priestly rituals could bring salvation.
  • Opposition to caste-based superiority: both admitted people of all varnas and stressed conduct over birth.
  • Ahimsa (non-violence): both made non-injury to living beings central; Mahavira took it further.
  • Karma and rebirth: both accepted that actions decide future births and that the cycle of rebirth is suffering.
  • Liberation through personal effort: nirvana (Buddha) and kaivalya/moksha (Mahavira) were to be gained by right conduct and knowledge, not by God's grace; neither gave importance to a creator god.
  • Ethical life: truth, non-stealing, non-attachment and self-control (the Jain mahavratas, the Buddha's panchashila).
  • Monastic orders: both founded orders (sangha) of monks and nuns with lay followers.
  • People's language: both preached in Prakrit languages — Pali (Buddha) and Ardhamagadhi (Mahavira).
  • Royal patronage from rulers of Magadha such as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru.

Both teachings made Indian religion more ethical, egalitarian and non-violent, and influenced later thinkers including Gandhi.

Childhood in Conflict Zones

A child in Gaza who counts drones instead of stars, a girl in Sudan who walks for days to a camp, a boy in eastern Ukraine who has spent two winters in a basement classroom — these are not rare stories. According to UNICEF, more than 470 million children, about one in six in the world, live in areas affected by conflict. Childhood, which should be a time of play, learning and safety, has become for them a time of fear, loss and survival.

What war takes from children

The most visible loss is life and limb. The UN's annual report on children and armed conflict now records more than 30,000 grave violations against children in a single year: killing and maiming, recruitment as soldiers, abduction, sexual violence, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian aid. Landmines and unexploded shells continue to kill children long after the guns fall silent.

War also destroys the systems that protect children. Schools are bombed or turned into shelters and barracks; teachers flee; examinations stop. Hospitals lose power and medicine, and vaccination campaigns collapse, so measles and polio return. Families are torn apart. Millions of children are displaced — they grow up in camps, cross borders alone, and fall prey to traffickers. Hunger follows conflict closely: famine conditions in parts of Sudan and Gaza have left children with stunted bodies and minds.

The deepest wound is often invisible. Children who have seen killing, lost parents or lived under bombardment carry trauma — nightmares, anxiety, aggression and withdrawal. Without care, this toxic stress affects brain development, learning and relationships for life. Child soldiers face a double burden: they are both victims and, in the eyes of their communities, perpetrators.

A lost generation and a cycle of violence

When a generation grows up without education, without health and with grief and anger, the cost falls on the whole society. Illiteracy, unemployment and resentment make young people easy recruits for armed groups, and the conflict feeds itself. Peace becomes harder, because reconciliation requires citizens who can imagine a future different from their past.

What exists to protect children

The world has built a framework. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), the most widely ratified human-rights treaty, and its Optional Protocol on children in armed conflict set 18 as the minimum age for direct participation in hostilities. International humanitarian law protects civilians, schools and hospitals. The Safe Schools Declaration commits states to keep schools out of military use. The UN Security Council's monitoring of "six grave violations" names the parties that harm children.

Yet these rules are often ignored. Accountability is weak, aid is blocked, and humanitarian appeals for education in emergencies receive only a small share of what is needed.

What must be done

First, prevention and accountability: parties to conflict must respect international law, and those who target children must face justice through national courts and international mechanisms.

Second, education cannot wait. Temporary learning spaces, radio and digital lessons, and teachers trained for crisis settings can keep learning alive. Education gives children routine, hope and protection from recruitment.

Third, mental-health and psychosocial support must be part of every humanitarian response — child-friendly spaces, trained counsellors and family tracing to reunite separated children.

Fourth, reintegration of former child soldiers through schooling, skills training and community acceptance, as tried in Sierra Leone and Colombia.

Fifth, funding and access: humanitarian corridors and predictable funding for nutrition, health and education.

India too has a role. Children in conflict-affected parts of our own country — in areas affected by insurgency or ethnic violence such as Manipur — need special care through schools, Child Welfare Committees under the Juvenile Justice Act and relief camps that respect their needs. Abroad, India's humanitarian aid and peacekeeping, where Indian troops and the women's units have protected civilians, show what responsible engagement can do.

Conclusion

Nelson Mandela said that there can be no keener revelation of a society's soul than the way in which it treats its children. Conflict zones reveal how often adults fail that test. Protecting childhood in war is not charity; it is an investment in peace. Every school kept open, every child reunited with a parent and every young mind helped to heal is a step towards ending the cycle of violence. The children who survive today's wars will build — or break — tomorrow's peace.

Wildlife Preservation and the Development Drive

India is one of the world's seventeen mega-diverse countries. With only 2.4% of the world's land, it holds about 7–8% of recorded species, including the largest populations of wild tigers and Asian elephants. India is also the world's most populous country and one of the fastest-growing major economies, building roads, railways, dams, mines and cities at great speed. The question of our time is whether these two facts can live together.

Why development presses on wildlife

Development needs land, water and energy. Highways and railway lines cut through forests and elephant corridors; hundreds of elephants have died on railway tracks in recent decades. Mining for coal, iron and bauxite removes forests in central India, the heart of tiger and elephant habitat. Dams submerge valleys, and urban growth swallows wetlands and grasslands. Habitat loss and fragmentation, rather than hunting, are now the biggest threats to wildlife. When habitats shrink, human–wildlife conflict rises: leopards in Mumbai's suburbs, elephants in Kerala's villages and tigers near farms in Maharashtra.

Why wildlife matters for development

Wildlife is not a luxury standing in the way of growth. Forests and wild areas provide water for rivers and cities, protect soil, store carbon and pollinate crops. Kaziranga's floodplains, the Sundarbans' mangroves and the Western Ghats' forests protect millions of people from floods, cyclones and drought. Wildlife tourism supports local jobs. Development that destroys these services is not development at all; it simply shifts costs onto the poor and the future.

India's record

India has shown that conservation can succeed even with large populations. Project Tiger (1973) has helped tiger numbers rise to over 3,600 (2022 estimate), about three-quarters of the world's wild tigers. The Asiatic lion has recovered in Gir; the one-horned rhino in Kaziranga. Laws such as the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, and a network of over a thousand protected areas, provide a strong base.

But there are worries. Amendments to forest laws in 2023, fast-tracked clearances and diversion of forest land for projects have raised concerns about weaker scrutiny. Projects such as the Ken–Betwa river link will submerge part of the Panna Tiger Reserve; the Great Nicobar project will clear tropical forest in a biodiversity-rich island. The challenge is not whether to develop but how.

Reconciling the two

The answer lies in smart, sustainable development:

  • Avoid, minimise, mitigate: avoid the most valuable habitats, and route roads and rail lines around them.
  • Green infrastructure: animal underpasses and overpasses, as on NH-44 through the Pench landscape, and speed limits on railway lines in elephant corridors.
  • Landscape planning: protect corridors that link reserves, not just islands of forest.
  • Honest environmental impact assessment with public hearings and independent monitoring.
  • Community partnership: recognise forest rights, share tourism revenue, and pay quick compensation for crop and livestock losses, so that local people become guardians of wildlife.
  • Compensatory afforestation that restores real ecosystems, not monoculture plantations.

Conclusion

Gandhi said the earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need, but not every man's greed. Wildlife preservation and development are not enemies; both aim at a better life for people. A growing India must build infrastructure, but it must build with care, so that the tiger, the elephant and the forests that sustain us all survive into the India of 2047.

RitaPrithvi SuktaAranyaniSacred groves

The Vedic world-view saw nature as a living, sacred order (Rita) of which humans are a part, not masters. This outlook produced a set of values and practices that match modern ideas of sustainable forest management.

1. Ideas in the texts

  • Earth as mother: the Prithvi Sukta of the Atharvaveda (12.1) says "the Earth is my mother and I am her son" and prays that what is dug from her may grow back quickly — an early idea of regeneration.
  • The forest as a deity: the Rigveda's hymn to Aranyani (10.146) praises the forest goddess who feeds all and harms none; trees are honoured as vanaspati.
  • Restraint in use: the Isha Upanishad's "enjoy through renunciation; do not covet" is a principle of taking only what is needed.
  • Forest as a place of learning: the Aranyakas and Upanishads were composed in forest hermitages, giving forests intellectual and spiritual value.

2. Practices that conserved forests

  • Sacred groves (devarakadu, orans, sarnas) left untouched for deities, still about 1 lakh in India.
  • Planting and protecting trees such as peepal, banyan and tulsi as religious duty.
  • Yajna as a cycle of giving back to nature; offerings to rivers, trees and animals.

3. Relevance today

These ideas support community forest management, Joint Forest Management, the protection of sacred groves as community reserves, and Mission LiFE's call for mindful consumption.

The Vedic stress on balance, reciprocity and restraint gives a cultural foundation for conserving forests, though it must be joined with modern science and secure rights for forest communities.

Panipat 1526VijayanagaraPortuguese in GoaRegional sultanates

The years 1500–1530 were a turning point in Indian political history: an old order in north India collapsed, a new empire was founded, the south reached its peak, and a European naval power arrived on the coast.

1. North India: from Sultanate to Mughals

  • The Lodi Sultanate weakened after Sikandar Lodi (d. 1517); Ibrahim Lodi alienated his Afghan nobles.
  • Babur defeated Ibrahim at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), using field artillery and the tulughma tactic, ending the Delhi Sultanate.
  • He defeated the Rajput confederacy of Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527) and the Afghans at Ghaghra (1529), laying the base of the Mughal Empire.

2. The South and the Deccan

  • Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) took Vijayanagara to its height: victories over Bijapur and the Gajapatis, Raichur (1520), and a rich court culture.
  • The Bahmani kingdom broke up into five Deccan sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Berar, Bidar).

3. Europeans at sea

  • Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510; the Portuguese controlled sea lanes through forts and the cartaz pass system. Sea power became decisive in Indian politics for the first time.

4. Regional powers

  • Mewar under Rana Sanga, Gujarat (Mahmud Begada to Bahadur Shah) and Bengal under Alauddin Husain Shah were strong regional states.

Together these events reshaped the balance of power: gunpowder warfare, Mughal centralisation and European maritime control shaped the next three centuries.
